etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English delicious, from Anglo-Norman delicious, from Old French delicious, delicieux, from Late Latin dēliciōsus (“delicate, delicious”), from dēliciae (“delights”), plural of dēlicia (“pleasure”), from deliciō (“I allure, I entice”), from de- (“away”) + laciō (“I lure, I deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. Displaced native Old English ārlīċ (“delicious”).

definitions.definition: Pleasing to the sense of taste; tasty.
(colloquial, figurative) Pleasing to a person's taste; pleasing to the eyes or mind.

quote.citation: 1986, Patrick Lichfield, Courvoisier's Book of the Best, page 230:
quote.text: But the houses are so delicious and the way they're townscaped on to hilly bits is absolutely wonderful.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Jones had not travelled far before he paid his compliments to that beautiful planet, and, turning to his companion, asked him if he had ever beheld so delicious an evening?
